$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. $n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any

$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$

so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Every subspace of a separable metric space is separable: take its countable base of intersections with ambient rational balls and, using [F5], choose one point from each nonempty intersection. Thus $H$ and $V$ are separable.

The $L^2$ and $H^1$ graph inner products make the ambient spaces Hilbert: completeness of $L^2$ and the Sobolev completeness in [F3] give convergence of Cauchy sequences in the function and all derivative coordinates, and the weak-derivative identity passes to the limit against each test. The $V$ norm dominates the $H$ norm; since $D_\sigma$ is dense in both closures, the inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$ is continuous with dense image.

Separability of $V$ and density of $D_\sigma$ in $V$ allow Countable Choice to select $d_j\in D_\sigma$ approximating a countable dense subset of $V$ to every rational precision; the selected countable collection is dense in $V$ and, because $D_\sigma$ is also dense in $H$, its linear span is dense in $H$. The space $D_\sigma$ is infinite dimensional: choose countably many disjoint balls in one ball contained in $\Omega$ and in each choose a nonzero smooth compactly supported curl field; their disjoint supports give linear independence. Apply Gram–Schmidt in $H$ to the selected collection, discarding zero remainders. Each resulting $e_j$ is a finite linear combination of elements of $D_\sigma$, so is still in $D_\sigma$; its span contains every selected $d_j$ after the corresponding finite stage and is therefore dense in $V$ and $H$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ (A function is a relation $f$ with $(a,b) \in f$ and $(a,c) \in f$ implying $b = c$; $f : A \to B$, the value $f(a)$, domain and codomain,
> The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann)) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** Choice function and
The Axiom of Choice select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$) does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ (The power set $\mathcal{P}(x) = \{\, z : z \subseteq x \,\}$, The Cartesian product $A \times B := \{\, z \in \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(A \cup B)) : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ z = (a,b) \,\}$, The Axiom Schema of Separation: for each formula $\varphi$, $\forall \bar p\,\forall x\,\exists y\,\forall z\,(z \in y \leftrightarrow (z \in x \wedge \varphi(z,\bar p)))$); a natural is the set of its predecessors (On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ (Every nonzero natural number is a successor); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction (The principle of mathematical induction), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. **$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense (Chain in a poset). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Choice, let $\nu>0$, and let $u_0\in H$ for the bounded closure spaces
defined above. There exists
$$u\in C_w([0,\infty);H)\cap L^\infty(0,\infty;H)\cap L^2_{\rm loc}(0,\infty;V)$$
with $u(0)=u_0$ and $\|u(t)-u_0\|_H\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, satisfying for
every compactly time-supported $C^1$ map $\phi:[0,\infty)\to V$,
$$\int_0^\infty\!\big[(u,\partial_t\phi)+(u\otimes u,\nabla\phi)-\nu(\nabla u,\nabla\phi)\big]dt+(u_0,\phi(0))=0.$$
It also satisfies
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_0^t\|\nabla u\|_2^2ds\le\|u_0\|_2^2\quad(t\ge0),$$
and there is a full-measure set $S\subset(0,\infty)$ such that for every
$s\in S\cup\{0\}$ and $t\ge s$,
$$\|u(t)\|_2^2+2\nu\int_s^t\|\nabla u\|_2^2d\tau\le\|u(s)\|_2^2.$$
The conclusion is a velocity result for the specified unforced closure-space
formulation; it asserts no uniqueness, smoothness, pressure regularity, or
boundary trace beyond membership in $H_0^1$. Here
$(u\otimes u):\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_j\phi_i$ and
$\nabla u:\nabla\phi=\sum_{i,j}\partial_j u_i\partial_j\phi_i$. For a matrix field
$A$, $(\operatorname{div}A)_i=\sum_j\partial_jA_{ij}$.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $\Omega=\prod_{i=1}^d(a_i,b_i)$ be a nonempty finite open rectangle. Write $D(\Omega)=C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $D_0(\Omega)=\{h\in D(\Omega):\int_\Omega h=0\}$. For every compact $K\subset\Omega$ there is a compact $K'\subset\Omega$ such that a linear map $R:D_0(\Omega)\to D(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$ sends tests supported in $K$ to fields supported in $K'$, satisfies $\operatorname{div}(Rh)=h$, and is continuous on each fixed-support test space for the seminorms $\sup|\partial^\alpha h|$.

For open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a **distribution** is a continuous complex-linear map $u:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to\mathbb C$, with the test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Their vector space is denoted $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. Write $\langle u,\varphi\rangle=u(\varphi)$; the pairing is linear in both arguments, with no conjugation.

Continuity means continuity for that topology: for each $\varepsilon>0$ the set $\{|u(\varphi)|<\varepsilon\}$ contains a zero-neighborhood. By linearity this suffices at every point. Sums and scalar multiples remain continuous and linear, so the indicated collection is a complex vector space. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, its test space is zero and its distribution space is zero as well. The finite-order estimate and the sequential criterion are established separately; neither substitutes for continuity in this definition.

For a distribution $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ in the convention of [[def-distribution]] and a multi-index $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, its **distributional derivative** is
$$\langle\partial^\alpha u,\varphi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle u,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle\qquad(\varphi\in\mathcal D(\Omega)).$$
The test derivative is a continuous linear endomorphism by [[thm-test-function-operations-are-continuous]]. Its composition with $u$, multiplied by the indicated sign, is therefore a continuous complex-linear functional, so this definition produces a distribution. The pairing is bilinear, with no complex conjugation. For $\alpha=0$ the operation is the identity; for one coordinate derivative its sign is minus. Every derivative of the zero distribution is zero, including on the empty domain. No choice axiom enters this construction. Compatibility with classical derivatives requires an integration-by-parts argument where it is used; it is not part of the definition.

The residual $T$ is a spacetime distribution: $u\in L^2_{\rm loc}$, $u\otimes u\in L^1_{\rm loc}$, and the second derivatives in $\Delta u$ act continuously on smooth tests by transferring derivatives. For a scalar test $\phi(t,x)$ put $\phi_0=\phi-\theta(x)\int_\Omega\phi(t,y)dy$ and define
$$\langle\pi,\phi\rangle=-\langle T,R_x\phi_0\rangle.$$
The map $R$ is applied at each time. Its fixed support and seminorm bounds in [F2] ensure $R_x\phi_0$ is a smooth spacetime test with the same compact temporal support; the fixed-interval formulas for $R$ commute with time derivatives by differentiation under the integral. Thus the displayed functional is continuous on test functions and is a distribution.

For a compact smooth vector test $\psi$, $h=\operatorname{div}_x\psi$ has spatial integral zero by coordinate integration, so $h\in D_0(\Omega)$ and $\psi-Rh$ is compactly supported, smooth, and divergence free. By [F1], $\langle T,\psi-Rh\rangle=0$. Moreover,
$$\langle\nabla_x\pi,\psi\rangle=-\langle\pi,h\rangle=\langle T,Rh\rangle=\langle T,\psi\rangle.$$
Substituting the definition of $T$ proves the full distributional momentum equation. The normalization holds because $(a\theta)_0=0$.

If $\pi_1,\pi_2$ have the same gradient, their difference $q$ annihilates every $h\in D_0$ since $h=\operatorname{div}Rh$ and $\langle q,h\rangle=-\langle\nabla q,Rh\rangle=0$. For an arbitrary scalar test $\phi$, $\phi-\theta\int_\Omega\phi$ lies in $D_0$, so $\langle q,\phi\rangle=\langle q,\theta\rangle\int_\Omega\phi$. Thus $q$ is a spatially constant distribution in time; the normalization forces $\langle q,a\theta\rangle=0$ for every temporal test $a$, so $q=0$. This proves uniqueness conditional on [F2].
